notes.summary: Trigonometry is the study of the six ratios of an angle in a right triangle. SSC asks 2 to 3 questions in Tier 1 and 3 to 5 in Tier 2, mostly on standard values, identities, complementary angles and heights and distances. Learn the value table, the three Pythagorean identities and ASTC, and most questions reduce to one or two lines.

concepts.title: The six ratios in a right triangle
concepts.body:
Trigonometry links the angles of a right triangle to its sides. Pick an acute angle θ. The side facing θ is the opposite, the side next to θ (not the longest) is the adjacent, and the longest side, facing the right angle, is the hypotenuse.

RatioMeaningReciprocal
sin θopposite / hypotenusecosec θ = hypotenuse / opposite
cos θadjacent / hypotenusesec θ = hypotenuse / adjacent
tan θopposite / adjacentcot θ = adjacent / opposite

Memory aid: SOH CAH TOA (Sin = Opp/Hyp, Cos = Adj/Hyp, Tan = Opp/Adj). Also tan θ = sin θ / cos θ and cot θ = cos θ / sin θ.

For an acute angle, sin θ and cos θ lie between 0 and 1, sec θ and cosec θ are 1 or more, and tan θ and cot θ can be any positive number.

concepts.title: Finding every ratio from one ratio
concepts.body:
If one ratio is given, draw a right triangle, put the two given numbers on the right sides, and find the third side by Pythagoras. Then read off any ratio.

Example: sin θ = 3/5. Opposite = 3, hypotenuse = 5, so adjacent = √(25 − 9) = 4. Now cos θ = 4/5, tan θ = 3/4, sec θ = 5/4.

Learn these Pythagorean triplets so you rarely need the square root:

TripletTripletTriplet
3, 4, 55, 12, 138, 15, 17
7, 24, 2520, 21, 299, 40, 41
12, 35, 3711, 60, 6128, 45, 53

Multiples also work: 6, 8, 10 and 9, 12, 15. For any odd number m, (m, (m2 − 1)/2, (m2 + 1)/2) is a triplet, for example 7, 24, 25.

Sides from a difference. In ΔABC right-angled at B with AB = 7 and AC − BC = 1: AC2 − BC2 = 49, so (AC − BC)(AC + BC) = 49 gives AC + BC = 49. So AC = 25, BC = 24.

Homogeneous expressions. If tan θ is given and the expression has the same power of sin and cos in every term, divide top and bottom by cos θ. For tan θ = 2/3: (3 sin θ − 4 cos θ)/(3 sin θ + 4 cos θ) = (3 tan θ − 4)/(3 tan θ + 4) = (2 − 4)/(2 + 4) = −1/3.

concepts.body:

Trick to rebuild the sin row: write √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2. The cos row is the same list backwards. Then tan = sin/cos, and the last three rows are reciprocals.

θ0°90°180°270°360°

Useful decimals: √2 ≈ 1.414, √3 ≈ 1.732, so sin 60° ≈ 0.866 and 1/√2 ≈ 0.707.

Example: tan(A + B) = √3 and tan(A − B) = 1/√3 give A + B = 60° and A − B = 30°, so A = 45° and B = 15°.

concepts.title: The three Pythagorean identities
concepts.body:
From opposite2 + adjacent2 = hypotenuse2, divide by different squares to get:

IdentityRearrangedFactored form
sin2θ + cos2θ = 1sin2θ = 1 − cos2θ(1 − sin θ)(1 + sin θ) = cos2θ
sec2θ − tan2θ = 1sec2θ = 1 + tan2θ(sec θ − tan θ)(sec θ + tan θ) = 1
cosec2θ − cot2θ = 1cosec2θ = 1 + cot2θ(cosec θ − cot θ)(cosec θ + cot θ) = 1

Most "simplify" questions are just these three, used after writing everything in sin and cos.

Note: sin2θ means (sin θ)2. It is not sin(θ2).

concepts.title: Results built from the identities
concepts.body:
• If sec θ + tan θ = p, then sec θ − tan θ = 1/p. Adding and subtracting: sec θ = (p + 1/p)/2, tan θ = (p − 1/p)/2, and sin θ = (p2 − 1)/(p2 + 1).
  • If cosec θ + cot θ = p, then cosec θ − cot θ = 1/p, and cos θ = (p2 − 1)/(p2 + 1).
  • (sin θ + cos θ)2 = 1 + 2 sin θ cos θ and (sin θ − cos θ)2 = 1 − 2 sin θ cos θ. So if sin θ + cos θ = p, then sin θ cos θ = (p2 − 1)/2.
  • sin4θ + cos4θ = 1 − 2 sin2θ cos2θ
  • sin6θ + cos6θ = 1 − 3 sin2θ cos2θ
  • sin4θ − cos4θ = sin2θ − cos2θ
  • tan θ + cot θ = sec θ cosec θ = 1/(sin θ cos θ)
  • sec2θ + cosec2θ = sec2θ cosec2θ
  • √((1 + sin θ)/(1 − sin θ)) = sec θ + tan θ and √((1 − sin θ)/(1 + sin θ)) = sec θ − tan θ (θ acute)
  • (tan θ + sec θ − 1)/(tan θ − sec θ + 1) = sec θ + tan θ = (1 + sin θ)/cos θ
  • If tan θ + cot θ = 2 (or sin θ + cosec θ = 2), then θ = 45° (or 90°), because x + 1/x = 2 only when x = 1.

Example: sec θ + tan θ = 2 gives sec θ − tan θ = 1/2, so sec θ = 5/4 and tan θ = 3/4.

concepts.title: Complementary angles
concepts.body:
Two angles are complementary when they add up to 90°. Each ratio of θ equals its "co" ratio of (90° − θ):

RatioEquals
sin(90° − θ)cos θ
cos(90° − θ)sin θ
tan(90° − θ)cot θ
cot(90° − θ)tan θ
sec(90° − θ)cosec θ
cosec(90° − θ)sec θ

So when A + B = 90°: sin A = cos B, tan A × tan B = 1, sin A sec B = 1, and sin2A + sin2B = 1.

Going the other way: if sin A = cos B with both acute, then A + B = 90°. For example sin(2x + 10°) = cos(3x − 20°) gives 5x − 10° = 90°, so x = 20°. Likewise tan(x + y) tan(x − y) = 1 gives 2x = 90°, so tan x = 1.

Long sums and products.

  • sin21° + sin22° + … + sin289° = 44.5 (44 pairs that each make 1, plus sin245° = 1/2).
  • sin25° + sin210° + … + sin285° = 8.5 (17 terms: 8 pairs plus 1/2).
  • tan 1° × tan 2° × … × tan 89° = 1 (each pair tan θ tan(90° − θ) = 1, and tan 45° = 1).
  • If a product contains cos 90° (or a sum contains a term that is 0 for another reason), it collapses to 0.

Example: sin 25° sin 65° − cos 25° cos 65° = sin 25° cos 25° − cos 25° sin 25° = 0.

concepts.title: Signs in the four quadrants and radians
concepts.body:
For angles beyond 90°, the ratio keeps its size but may change sign. Remember ASTC ("All Students Take Coffee"), going anticlockwise from 0°:

QuadrantAnglesPositive ratios
First0° to 90°All
Second90° to 180°sin and cosec
Third180° to 270°tan and cot
Fourth270° to 360°cos and sec

How to reduce any angle.

  1. Remove full turns: subtract 360° as many times as needed (1125° = 3 × 360° + 45°).
  2. Negative angles: sin(−θ) = −sin θ, cos(−θ) = cos θ, tan(−θ) = −tan θ.
  3. Write the angle as 180° ± θ or 360° − θ: the ratio stays the same. Write it as 90° ± θ or 270° ± θ: the ratio changes (sin ↔ cos, tan ↔ cot, sec ↔ cosec).
  4. Put the sign of the original ratio in the quadrant where the angle lies.

Examples: cos 120° = cos(180° − 60°) = −cos 60° = −1/2 (second quadrant, cos is negative). sin 150° = sin 30° = 1/2. tan 300° = −tan 60° = −√3. tan(−1125°) = −tan 1125° = −tan 45° = −1.

Degrees and radians.

π radians = 180°. To change degrees to radians multiply by π/180; radians to degrees multiply by 180/π.

Degrees30°45°60°90°120°180°270°360°
Radiansπ/6π/4π/3π/22π/3π3π/22π

1 radian ≈ 57.3°. In a circle, arc length = radius × angle (in radians).

Example: cos(−17π/3) = cos(17π/3). 17π/3 = 17 × 60° = 1020° = 2 × 360° + 300°, and cos 300° = cos 60° = 1/2.

concepts.title: Compound angle formulas
concepts.body:
• sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B
  • sin(A − B) = sin A cos B − cos A sin B
  • cos(A + B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B
  • cos(A − B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B
  • tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 − tan A tan B)
  • tan(A − B) = (tan A − tan B)/(1 + tan A tan B)

Spot them in reverse: cos 75° cos 15° − sin 75° sin 15° = cos 90° = 0, and sin 50° cos 40° + cos 50° sin 40° = sin 90° = 1.

Two products asked often: sin A sin(60° − A) sin(60° + A) = (1/4) sin 3A, and tan A tan(60° − A) tan(60° + A) = tan 3A.

Remember that sin(A + B) is not sin A + sin B. Check with A = B = 45°: sin 90° = 1, but sin 45° + sin 45° = √2.

concepts.title: Double angles and special values
concepts.body:
• sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A = 2 tan A/(1 + tan2A)
  • cos 2A = cos2A − sin2A = 2cos2A − 1 = 1 − 2sin2A = (1 − tan2A)/(1 + tan2A)
  • tan 2A = 2 tan A/(1 − tan2A)
  • sin 3A = 3 sin A − 4 sin3A and cos 3A = 4 cos3A − 3 cos A
  • 1 + cos 2A = 2cos2A and 1 − cos 2A = 2sin2A
AngleValue
sin 15° = cos 75°(√3 − 1)/(2√2)
cos 15° = sin 75°(√3 + 1)/(2√2)
tan 15° = cot 75°2 − √3
tan 75° = cot 15°2 + √3
tan 22.5°√2 − 1
sin 18° = cos 72°(√5 − 1)/4
cos 36° = sin 54°(√5 + 1)/4

Example: tan 15° + tan 75° = (2 − √3) + (2 + √3) = 4.

concepts.title: Value-putting method
concepts.body:
When an identity question has options and the answer does not depend on θ, put a simple angle (0°, 30°, 45°, 60° or 90°) into the question and pick the option that matches.

  • Choose an angle that keeps every term defined. Avoid 90° if tan or sec appears, and 0° if cot or cosec appears.
  • If the condition fixes θ (for example tan θ + cot θ = 2 means θ = 45°), put that angle in.
  • If the answer still depends on θ, put the same angle into each option too. If two options tie, try a second angle.

Example: (sin θ + cos θ)2 + (sin θ − cos θ)2. Put θ = 0°: (0 + 1)2 + (0 − 1)2 = 2. The answer is 2 for every θ.

concepts.body:
ExpressionMinimumMaximum
sin θ, cos θ−11

a sin2θ + b cos2θsmaller of a and blarger of a and b
sin θ cos θ−1/21/2
a2tan2θ + b2cot2θ2abno maximum
sec2θ + cosec2θ4no maximum

Why 2ab? For two positive terms whose product is fixed, the sum is least when the terms are equal: x + y ≥ 2√(xy). Example: 25 cos2x + 9 sec2x ≥ 2√(25 × 9) = 30, reached when 25 cos2x = 9 sec2x, that is cos2x = 3/5, which is possible.

Check that the equal point is possible. For 9 cos2x + 25 sec2x, equality needs cos2x = 5/3, which is impossible, so the least value is at cos2x = 1: 9 + 25 = 34.

Example: the greatest value of 5 sin θ + 12 cos θ is √(25 + 144) = 13.

concepts.title: Heights and distances: the basics
concepts.body:
• Angle of elevation: you look up at an object; the angle is measured from the horizontal line at your eye.
  • Angle of depression: you look down; the angle is measured from the horizontal line at your eye, not from the vertical.
  • The angle of depression from A to B equals the angle of elevation from B to A (alternate angles).
  • Towers, poles and buildings stand vertically, so each picture is a right triangle. Use tan θ = height / base most of the time.
AngleHeight : baseHeight : slant line
30°1 : √31 : 2
45°1 : 11 : √2
60°√3 : 1√3 : 2

Example: a tower is seen at 60° from 30 m away. Height = 30 × tan 60° = 30√3 m ≈ 51.96 m.

concepts.title: Heights and distances: two angles
concepts.body:
Same side. From D the top is seen at β, and after walking d towards the tower to C it is seen at α (α > β). Then

h = d × tan α × tan β / (tan α − tan β)

AnglesHeight h
30° and 60°d × √3/2
30° and 45°d × (√3 + 1)/2
45° and 60°d × (3 + √3)/2

For the same height, the distance at 30° is 3 times the distance at 60°. So with 30° and 60°, the walk d = 2x, where x is the near distance.

Shadow problems work the same way: the sun's altitude is the angle of elevation and the shadow is the base. When the altitude falls from 45° to 30°, the shadow grows by h(√3 − 1).

Example: d = 20 m, angles 30° and 60°. h = 20 × √3/2 = 10√3 m ≈ 17.32 m.

concepts.title: Heights and distances: opposite sides and depression
concepts.body:
Objects on opposite sides. From the top of a lighthouse of height h, two ships on opposite sides are seen at depressions α and β. The distance between the ships = h(cot α + cot β).

Example: h = 100 m, depressions 30° and 45°: distance = 100(√3 + 1) ≈ 273.2 m.

Both on the same side (ship moving towards the lighthouse): distance moved = h(cot β − cot α), where β is the smaller angle.

Building and tower. From the top of a building of height h, the top of a taller tower is seen at elevation α and its foot at depression β. The gap between them is x = h cot β, and the tower height = h + x tan α.

concepts.title: Angles of a triangle in trigonometry
concepts.body:
In any ΔABC, A + B + C = 180°. So:

  • sin(A + B) = sin C and cos(A + B) = −cos C, tan(A + B) = −tan C
  • sin((A + B)/2) = cos(C/2) and cos((A + B)/2) = sin(C/2)
  • In a right triangle with right angle at B: A + C = 90°, so sin A = cos C and tan A tan C = 1.

Example: ABC right-angled at B with tan A = √3, so A = 60° and C = 30°. Then sin A cos C + cos A sin C = sin(A + C) = sin 90° = 1, and cos A cos C − sin A sin C = cos 90° = 0.

varieties.name: Ratios from one given ratio
varieties.how: Draw a right triangle, write the two known sides from the given ratio, find the third by Pythagoras (or a triplet), then read off the ratio you need. If tan θ is given and every term has sin or cos to the same power, divide top and bottom by cos θ.

example.q: In ΔABC, right-angled at B, AB = 7 cm and AC − BC = 1 cm. Find sec C + cot A.
steps: AC<sup>2</sup> − BC<sup>2</sup> = AB<sup>2</sup> = 49, so (AC − BC)(AC + BC) = 49
AC − BC = 1 gives AC + BC = 49, so AC = 25 and BC = 24
sec C = AC/BC = 25/24 and cot A = AB/BC = 7/24

varieties.name: Standard angle values
varieties.how: Replace each ratio by its table value, then simplify. If an equation gives tan(A + B) or similar as a table value, turn it into an angle equation and solve.

example.q: If tan(A + B) = √3 and tan(A − B) = 1/√3, with 0° < A + B ≤ 90° and A > B, find A and B.

varieties.name: Simplifying identities
varieties.how: Write everything in sin and cos, take an LCM, and use sin<sup>2</sup>θ + cos<sup>2</sup>θ = 1 (or its sec–tan and cosec–cot forms). With options, the value-putting method (θ = 30°, 45° or 60°) is often fastest.

example.q: If (tan θ + sin θ)/(tan θ − sin θ) = (k + 1)/(k − 1), find k.
steps: Divide top and bottom by sin θ: (1/cos θ + 1)/(1/cos θ − 1)

varieties.name: Given a condition, find a value
varieties.how: Use the factored identities: if sec θ + tan θ = p then sec θ − tan θ = 1/p; if sin θ + cos θ = p then sin θ cos θ = (p<sup>2</sup> − 1)/2. Square or subtract the given equations so that a Pythagorean identity appears. If the condition fixes θ, find θ and substitute.

example.q: If a cot θ + b cosec θ = p and b cot θ + a cosec θ = q, find p<sup>2</sup> − q<sup>2</sup>.
steps: p<sup>2</sup> = a<sup>2</sup>cot<sup>2</sup>θ + 2ab cot θ cosec θ + b<sup>2</sup>cosec<sup>2</sup>θ
q<sup>2</sup> = b<sup>2</sup>cot<sup>2</sup>θ + 2ab cot θ cosec θ + a<sup>2</sup>cosec<sup>2</sup>θ
p<sup>2</sup> − q<sup>2</sup> = a<sup>2</sup>(cot<sup>2</sup>θ − cosec<sup>2</sup>θ) + b<sup>2</sup>(cosec<sup>2</sup>θ − cot<sup>2</sup>θ)

varieties.name: Complementary angles
varieties.how: Pair each angle with the one that makes 90° and swap the ratio for its co-ratio (sin ↔ cos, tan ↔ cot, sec ↔ cosec). If sin A = cos B or tan A tan B = 1 for acute angles, then A + B = 90°.

example.q: If sin(2x + 10°) = cos(3x − 20°), where both angles are acute, find x.
steps: sin A = cos B with both acute means A + B = 90°

varieties.name: Compound and double angles
varieties.how: Recognise the pattern sin A cos B ± cos A sin B or cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B and fold it into one angle. Break awkward angles into standard ones (75° = 45° + 30°, 15° = 45° − 30°).

example.q: Find the value of tan 15° + tan 75°.

varieties.name: Angles beyond 90° and radians
varieties.how: Convert radians to degrees (π = 180°), remove full turns of 360°, handle the minus sign (only cos and sec ignore it), write the angle as 180° ± θ or 360° − θ (same ratio) or 90° ± θ, 270° ± θ (co-ratio), then fix the sign with ASTC.

varieties.name: Maximum and minimum values
varieties.how: For a sin θ + b cos θ the range is ±√(a<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup>). For two positive terms whose product is constant (like tan<sup>2</sup> and cot<sup>2</sup>, or cos<sup>2</sup> and sec<sup>2</sup>), the least sum is 2√(product), but only if the equal point is possible. For a sin<sup>2</sup>θ + b cos<sup>2</sup>θ the answer lies between a and b.

example.q: Find the minimum value of 25 cos<sup>2</sup>x + 9 sec<sup>2</sup>x.
steps: The product 25 cos<sup>2</sup>x × 9 sec<sup>2</sup>x = 225 is constant
That needs cos<sup>2</sup>x = 3/5, which is possible, so 30 is reached

varieties.name: Heights and distances
varieties.how: Draw the figure: ground horizontal, tower vertical, sight line slanting. Mark the angle at the observer (for depression, at the top, from the horizontal). Write tan θ = height/base for each right triangle and solve. Use the 30°, 45°, 60° ratios 1 : √3, 1 : 1, √3 : 1 directly.

example.q: The shadow of a vertical tower on level ground grows by 8.4 m when the sun's altitude changes from 45° to 30°. Find the height of the tower.
steps: At 45° the shadow is h; at 30° the shadow is h√3

tips: Learn the triplets 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25 and 20-21-29. Most "given one ratio" questions use them.
If tan θ is given, divide the expression top and bottom by cos θ instead of finding sin and cos separately.
In identity questions with options, put θ = 45° (or 30°, 60°) and check the options. It is faster than simplifying.
See sec θ + tan θ or cosec θ + cot θ? Their partner difference is the reciprocal. That one fact solves many questions.
Look for angle pairs that add to 90°. A long sum of sin<sup>2</sup> terms is half the number of terms; a long product of tan terms is 1.
In heights and distances, the same height seen at 30° and 60° gives distances in the ratio 3 : 1.
tan 15° = 2 − √3 and tan 75° = 2 + √3. Their product is 1 and their sum is 4.
traps: The angle of depression is measured from the horizontal at the observer's eye, not from the tower.
sin(A + B) is not sin A + sin B, and sin 2θ is not 2 sin θ.
tan 90° and sec 90° are not defined. Do not put θ = 90° (or 0° for cot and cosec) in the value-putting method.
After reducing a large or negative angle, take the sign from the quadrant of the original angle, not of the reduced one.
The "2√(product)" minimum works only if the equal point is possible. 9 cos<sup>2</sup>x + 25 sec<sup>2</sup>x has least value 34, not 30.

formulas.name: Basic ratios
formulas.expr: sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj

formulas.name: Reciprocals
formulas.expr: cosec = 1/sin, sec = 1/cos, cot = 1/tan

formulas.name: Pythagorean identity
formulas.expr: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1

formulas.name: Secant identity
formulas.expr: sec²θ − tan²θ = 1, so (sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ − tan θ) = 1

formulas.name: Cosecant identity
formulas.expr: cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1, so (cosec θ + cot θ)(cosec θ − cot θ) = 1

formulas.name: Complementary angles
formulas.expr: sin(90° − θ) = cos θ, tan(90° − θ) = cot θ, sec(90° − θ) = cosec θ

formulas.name: Negative angles
formulas.expr: sin(−θ) = −sin θ, cos(−θ) = cos θ, tan(−θ) = −tan θ

formulas.name: Degree and radian
formulas.expr: π radians = 180°

formulas.name: sin of a sum
formulas.expr: sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B

formulas.name: cos of a sum
formulas.expr: cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B

formulas.name: tan of a sum
formulas.expr: tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B)/(1 ∓ tan A tan B)

formulas.name: Double angle
formulas.expr: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A, cos 2A = 1 − 2sin²A = 2cos²A − 1

formulas.name: Triple angle
formulas.expr: sin 3A = 3 sin A − 4 sin³A, cos 3A = 4 cos³A − 3 cos A

formulas.name: Fourth powers
formulas.expr: sin⁴θ + cos⁴θ = 1 − 2 sin²θ cos²θ

formulas.name: Sixth powers
formulas.expr: sin⁶θ + cos⁶θ = 1 − 3 sin²θ cos²θ

formulas.name: Range of a sin θ + b cos θ
formulas.expr: −√(a² + b²) to √(a² + b²)

formulas.name: Least value of a² tan²θ + b² cot²θ
formulas.expr: 2ab

formulas.name: Height
formulas.expr: h = base × tan θ

formulas.name: Two angles, same side
formulas.expr: h = d tan α tan β / (tan α − tan β)

formulas.name: Two objects, opposite sides
formulas.expr: distance = h(cot α + cot β)

questions.q: What is the value of sin 30° + cos 60°?
If sin θ = 3/5 and θ is acute, then tan θ is:
If sec θ + tan θ = 5, then sec θ is:
questions.solution:
(sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ − tan θ) = 1 → sec θ − tan θ = 1/5.
Adding: 2 sec θ = 5 + 1/5 = 26/5.
sec θ = 13/5.

questions.q: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point 30 m away from its foot on level ground is 60°. What is the height of the tower?
From the top of a building 60 m high, the angle of depression of a car changes from 30° to 45° as the car moves straight towards the building. How far did the car move?
questions.solution:
At 30°: distance = 60/tan 30° = 60√3 m.
At 45°: distance = 60/tan 45° = 60 m.
Distance moved = 60√3 − 60 = 60(√3 − 1) m ≈ 43.9 m.

questions.q: What is the value of sin<sup>2</sup>1° + sin<sup>2</sup>2° + sin<sup>2</sup>3° + … + sin<sup>2</sup>89°?
questions.solution:
Pair sin2θ with sin2(90° − θ) = cos2θ: each pair (1°, 89°), …, (44°, 46°) gives 1 → 44 pairs = 44.
Middle term sin245° = 1/2.
Total = 44 + 1/2 = 89/2.

flashcards.front: sec θ − tan θ if sec θ + tan θ = k
